title: Infra engineering consolidated playbook: GPU fleet, accounts, IaC, CI/CD, and runbooks
author: Marco Nguyen
content:
Purpose and scope

This consolidated playbook documents the conventions, runbooks, and operational practices for Redwood Inference infrastructure engineering. It covers: GPU fleet and capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/IaC module standards, CI/CD and build pipelines for infra, and core runbooks. This page is the canonical entry point for on-call, onboarding, and module authors.

Audience
- Infra engineers
- SREs and platform engineers
- Applied ML engineers who operate private/dedicated deployments

Owners and escalation
- Primary owner: infra-engineering team (engineering)
- On-call escalation: infra SRE rotation -> Platform lead -> Head of Infrastructure
- Pager duty: infra-oncall@redwood (see runbook links in related_pages)

Table of contents
1) GPU fleet & capacity planning
2) Cloud accounts & networking baseline
3) Terraform / IaC module standards
4) CI/CD & build for infra modules
5) Runbooks (incidents and operational playbooks)
6) Team wiki & contribution process
7) References and links

---

1) GPU fleet & capacity planning

Overview
- Purpose: provide reliable, cost-effective GPU capacity for hosted/dedicated/private inference.
- Fleet model: mixed-instance GPU pools split by workload class: interactive (low-latency), batch (high-throughput), and model-training/ops.

Node types and naming
- g4dn-type (low-latency, 1–2 models, 16GB KV cache)
- p4a-type (high-throughput, 80GB, optimized kernels)
- q8-small (quantized hosting nodes)
- Naming convention: infra-gpu-{region}-{purpose}-{size} (e.g., infra-gpu-us-west-interactive-p4a)

Capacity planning and targets
- Target headroom: 20% spare capacity for interactive pools during 95th percentile traffic.
- Scale policy: maintain at least 5 nodes for redundancy per region for interactive pools.
- SLOs: 99.9% requests served under 200ms per-token median for interactive; 99% under 300ms 95th.

Capacity thresholds (operational table)
| Metric | Warning | Critical | Action |
|--------|---------|----------|--------|
| GPU utilization (avg over 5m) | 60% | 85% | Warn: evaluate scaling; Critical: trigger autoscale + capacity request |
| Queue length (requests waiting) | 20 | 50 | Increase replicas / divert to best-effort pool |
| Prefix cache hit rate | 70% | 50% | Re-evaluate cache warming and model placement |

Autoscaling and burst capacity
- Autoscaler parameters are defined in terraform module infra-gpu-autoscaler. Typical settings: min_replicas=2, max_replicas=200, target_utilization=0.6.
- Burst capacity: reserved warm nodes (dedicated) for enterprise customers. To add burst capacity, open capacity request PR and notify capacity-planning channel.

Scheduling, eviction, and QoS
- Interactive pods run with qos: guaranteed; requests set limits/requests for CPU/GPU memory.
- Eviction policy: preemptible batch nodes first; interactive pools use graceful drain (max 60s) and fallback to model-variant routing.

Monitoring and alerts (what to watch)
- Metrics: gpu_utilization, gpu_mem_used, request_latency_p50/p95, queue_length, prefix_cache_hit_rate.
- Dashboards: /dashboards/gpu-fleet-overview, per-region dashboards under eng-platform.
- Alerts: GPU_UTIL_HIGH (avg>85% 5m), QUEUE_BACKLOG_HIGH (queue>50 3m), CACHE_DEGRADATION (hit_rate<50% 10m).

Operational play: capacity shortage
1. Confirm alerts and correlate with recent deploys (CI/CD run history).
2. If shortage in single region, failover traffic to nearest region via smart-routing policy.
3. Increase pool size via terraform var override + apply (fast path: trigger autoscaler increase via infra control plane).
4. Notify stakeholders and open incident if service impact > 5 minutes.

---

2) Cloud accounts & networking baseline

Account structure
- Primary AWS org structure:
  - prod (owned by infra-prod account)
  - staging
  - dev
  - shared-services (logging, CI/CD runners, artifact registry)
- Account naming: rw-<env>-<purpose> (e.g., rw-prod-gpu, rw-shared-ci).

VPC and subnet patterns
- Per-region VPC per environment with public/private subnets: rw-vpc-{env}-{region}.
- Private subnets host compute; public subnets host NAT + bastion as required.
- Use AWS Transit Gateway for multi-account networking to shared-services.

Cross-account roles and IAM
- Standard cross-account role names: InfraCrossAccountRole, ReadOnlyAuditRole.
- Least-privilege: modules must define only required actions; avoid wildcard resources.

Networking controls for GPU infra
- Use VPC endpoints for S3, ECR, and KMS.
- Restrict egress to allowed external services; use egress proxy in shared-services for audit.
- Recommended security groups: allow control-plane traffic from control plane CIDR and internal services only.

Bastion and emergency access
- Bastion is session-managed via SSM Session Manager; avoid long-lived SSH keys.
- Emergency break-glass is a documented process involving security approval and time-limited role elevation.

Compliance & data residency notes
- For private deployments, ensure customer VPC peering is documented in deployment ticket and appropriate ACLs/KMS keys are used.

---

3) Terraform / IaC module standards

Module registry and repos
- Repo: github.com/redwood-infra/terraform-modules (single repo, multiple modules).
- Registry naming: rw-terraform-<module-name>.

Module lifecycle and versioning
- Semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). Major bumps for breaking changes.
- Release process: PR -> CI tests -> tag -> publish to registry. Include CHANGELOG entry.

Standards and required outputs
- Modules must be: parameterized, idempotent, documented with examples, and support `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` configurable flag where destructive behavior is risky.
- Required outputs: resource_ids, primary_ip, resource_arn (strings).

Testing and verification
- Unit testing with terratest or kitchen-terraform in CI.
- Acceptance tests run against a disposable RW sandbox account. Failure blocks merge.

Example module usage (snippet)
```hcl
module "gpu_pool" {
  source  = "github.com/redwood-infra/terraform-modules//gpu-pool"
  version = "v1.2.0"

  region        = "us-west-2"
  pool_name     = "interactive-p4a"
  min_nodes     = 3
  max_nodes     = 200
  instance_type = "p4a.24xlarge"
}
```

Change/upgrade process
1. Open RFC for major changes to modules used by multiple teams.
2. Create branch and update module.
3. Run full CI (plan + terratest) and run in staging.
4. Coordinate rollout with owners and schedule maintenance window if required.

Policy: No direct changes to prod modules without at least two approvers and a successful staging rollout.

---

4) CI/CD & build for infra modules

Pipeline roles
- Plan pipeline: runs terraform fmt, init, validate, and terraform plan. Produces plan artifact and cost estimate.
- Apply pipeline: gated by approvals or automatic for non-prod; runs terraform apply with state lock.
- Testing pipeline: executes terratest/kitchen acceptance tests; publishes test results.

GitHub Actions sample (abridged)
```yaml
name: Infra CI
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Setup Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2
      - name: Terraform Init
        run: terraform init
      - name: Terraform Plan
        run: terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan
      - name: Upload Plan
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: plan
          path: plan.tfplan
  test:
    needs: plan
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Run terratest
        run: make test-acceptance
```

Approval policy
- Prod applies require at least two approvers from the owning team and one SRE oncall sign-off. Use CODEOWNERS to enforce.

Secrets and artifact handling
- Secrets are stored in HashiCorp Vault with env profiles bound to pipeline runners. Tokens for long-lived operations must be rotated and audited.

Drift detection
- Weekly drift job runs terraform plan against prod state and opens a PR for drift changes if any non-trivial diff exists. Critical drifts (network/security) open an incident.

---

5) Runbooks (incidents and operational playbooks)

GPU OOM / Model crash runbook (summary)
1. Pager triggers on MODEL_CRASH_HIGH or GPU_MEM_OOM.
2. Triage: identify model, container logs, and recent deploys. `kubectl logs -n inference <pod>`; check kube events.
3. If single pod: restart pod (kubectl delete pod) and monitor; roll back recent model deployment if repeated failures.
4. If fleet-wide: scale down traffic to affected model via routing policy to fallback variant; open incident and engage ML-engineering.
5. Post-incident: capture heap dump, upload to secure artifact store, and create regression ticket (assign to model-owner).

Capacity shortage runbook (summary)
1. Confirm alerts and identify affected pools.
2. Attempt autoscaler increase; if blocked, request hot capacity from cloud provider via capacity playbook (contact cloud-ops).
3. If critical, enable cross-region failover for impacted customers and notify CS/Account teams.

Account compromise suspected
1. Immediately rotate cross-account roles and revoke sessions.
2. Engage Security and run forensic playbook (see security-and-compliance incident-response-security).
3. Snapshot state and preserve logs for audit.

Operational checklist for any incident
- Triage and assign severity
- Run the relevant runbook steps
- Notify stakeholders (channel, pager, incident doc)
- Postmortem within 72 hours for any Sev>=2

---

6) Team wiki & contribution process

How to contribute
- Fork-and-PR model for docs and modules. Small changes can be merged with 1 reviewer; infra-wide changes require 2 reviewers and at least one SRE.
- Use templates: /confluence/templates/infra-change-request and /confluence/templates/module-release.

Onboarding checklist for new infra engineer
- Access: request infra GitHub, AWS sandbox, PagerDuty, Slack channels (#infra, #capacity-planning).
- Read: this playbook, GPU runbook, terraform module guidelines, CI/CD doc.
- Hands-on: runbook drill (game-day) and create a sandbox module PR.

Documentation hygiene
- Keep docs up to date with code changes (link PRs in doc updates).
- Use labels for doc pages: gpu-fleet, terraform, runbooks.

---

7) References and quick links
- GPU fleet dashboards: /dashboards/gpu-fleet-overview
- Terraform modules repo: https://github.com/redwood-infra/terraform-modules
- CI templates: /confluence/eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build/ci-templates
- Runbooks: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks
- Security incident response: /confluence/security-and-compliance/incident-response-security

Appendix: quick commands and snippets
- Check GPU utilization:
  - kubectl top nodes | grep gpu
  - aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --metric-name GPUUtilization --namespace RW/GPU --start-time ...
- Fast-scale autoscaler (example):
  - terraform apply -target=module.gpu_pool.aws_autoscaling_group.main -var='min_nodes=5'

Contact and feedback
- For questions about this playbook open an issue in the infra-team-wiki repo or message #infra in Slack.
- This document is reviewed quarterly; to request changes file a PR against the team-wiki.
